newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's ex-drug czar blasts new anti-drug unit.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's ex-drug czar blasts new anti-drug unit.

text.p: In an interview published on Friday Mexico's former drug czar blasted the scrapping of the agency he once headed as a "publicity coup" that will lead to hundreds of former drug agents going to work for drug cartels.
Mexico on Wednesday said its scandal-marred National Institute for Drug Combat (INCD) would be replaced by a new office called the Special Prosecutor's Office for Crimes Against Health.
U.S. President Bill Clinton, who will visit Mexico next week, praised the decision, calling it a "good first step."
But Francisco Molina Ruiz, who was commissioner of the INCD from March 1996 to December 1996, told Reforma newspaper that the move was "nothing more than a name change."

"This is nothing more than a publicity coup that could possibly temper the certification problem or gain votes for the next certification," Molina said, referring to the U.S. process of certifying whether Mexico is an aid-worthy ally in the war on drugs.

"It is a totally weakened force," Molina said of the new office, which is starting operations with 60 highly trained and scrupulously watched agents compared to the 1,200 agents of the notoriously corrupt INCD.
"What's going to happen to those 1,200?" Molina asked. "Are they going to throw them out in the street? Well, they're going to go over to the drug traffickers. That's the first problem."

In announcing the new office, Attorney General Jorge Madrazo Cuellar said anti-drug agents would have to pass rigorous drug and psychological tests in order to be hired. Of 107 former INCD agents who took the entrance exams, only 60 passed, Madrazo said.
Molina said that the 1,200 agents of the INCD were not enough to cover Mexican territory.
"How, then, is the special prosecutor going to operate with an elite corps of super-honest agents?" Molina said.
Molina was relieved of his post after former Attorney General Antonio Lozano Gracia was sacked on Dec. 2, 1996.
Molina was replaced by Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo, who just two months later was arrested on charges that he was on the payroll of the country's most-wanted drug baron, Amado Carrillo Fuentes.
Mexican officials said the old office was corrupt and inefficient when they announced the radical changes on Wednesday.
Molina said he also contemplated dismantling the INCD while he was in charge but that a team of experts studying the proposal, "concluded that it would be contradictory."
